Until now, one clause at a time. Real speech chains events: and, then, so, or, but. Gupapuyŋu has five small joiners, and one genuinely brilliant rule.

The five:
ga → and
bala → and then, so (sequence, one thing flowing into the next)
bili → so, and so (yes, bili again, chameleon face six)
ŋanydja → or, but
yurru → but

Ŋayi guya nhäŋala ga dharpuŋala → He saw the fish and speared it

(Notice: no repeated he in the second half. Subject said once, understood after. And you can even drop the joiner entirely and just lay clauses side by side, storytellers do it constantly.)

The two buts, and the rule I love:
English has one but. Gupapuyŋu has two, and chooses by logic:

If the first clause is negative, or holds a maybe (balaŋu, yanapi), the but is ŋanydja:
Ŋayi balaŋu ŋäṉ'thuna ŋanydja ŋayi yaka marrtjinya → He should have asked, but he didn't come

If the first clause is positive and factual, the but is yurru:
Ŋarra djäl dhiyaki yikiwa yurru ŋarra rrupiyamiriw → I want that knife, but I have no money

Feel the difference? ŋanydja contradicts a doubt or an absence; yurru pushes against a solid fact. The grammar tracks the epistemic weather of the sentence. English makes you guess from tone; here it's encoded.

Or, between words:
Between clauses, or is ŋanydja. But between mere words, you say maku, seasoned with a question word matching what kind of thing you're choosing between:
Ŋarra dhu yiki märrama nhä maku makarrpuy → I'll get a knife or (what-or) some trousers
Boŋa dhu marrtji yol maku Lorru → Boŋa or (who-or) Lorru will go
Märrma' maku ḻurrkun → two or three

What-or for things, who-or for people. Even or knows whether it's choosing between objects or humans.

Bonus: the sound-effect words:
And since we're chaining actions, meet the interjections, tiny invariant words, each married to a verb, that punch the action: dharr (seeing!), ḏutj (back again!), ḻarr' (off they go!), djip (put!), dhut (sit!), baṯ (hold!).
Dharrnha nhäŋuna! → Look!
Ŋayi marrtjina dhakallili ga ḏutj roŋiyina → He went to the island and, ḏutj, came back

They never conjugate. They're pure gesture in sound, the comic-book POW! of the language, except ancient, precise, and completely standard grammar. A story told with ḻarr' and ḏutj doesn't describe movement. It performs it.
